---
name: independent-ac-verifier
description: "Use when a managed task needs a separate acceptance judgment against the original request, current contract and actual profile-specific evidence."
---

# Independent acceptance

When `lead_review` is present, judge the original lead's classification and critiques.
Check omitted requirements, unsupported claims, stale evidence and unresolved
material findings. A cosmetic P3 is advisory. Generic summaries cannot pass.
A justified mechanical exemption needs no lead passes. Keep criterion IDs and wording.

Apply relevant [evidence decisions](../task-orchestrator/references/evidence-decisions.md): actual target/reference authority, required dependency postconditions and current artifact purpose/version. For migration/optimization assess meaningful equivalence and relevant boundaries/preexisting ambiguity. Metadata or prepared drafts are not consumer/execution evidence. Missing relevant code is a coverage gap to investigate or disclose; it does not establish absent behavior.

Act in a separate session from implementation. Read the original request and sources, approved proposal and stages, acceptance obligations, current artifacts and actual executed evidence. In a host request, `handoff.task_proposal` supplies the exact saved proposal and the stages actually approved (`approved_stage_ids`). Its `ancestor_proposals` list supplies relevant parent decisions for the linked stages. Apply those decisions within the child scope, including clarifications absent from the original ticket. Inspect the delivered result directly; an implementation summary is only a locator.

For each criterion report its ID, expected behavior, source/evidence references, verification method, PASS/FAIL/UNVERIFIED/BLOCKED/NOT_APPLICABLE, limitations and missing coverage. Mandatory unexecuted checks cannot PASS. Do not weaken acceptance to fit the implementation or infer a real resource/document/model run from a fixture.

When a defect outside the task (not in the ticket, not caused by the change) blocks the literal check of a denial or other negative criterion, judge the criterion's goal: a deliberate refusal by a working control (4xx authentication or authorization, no data returned; never a 5xx, timeout, crash or empty 200, for example 401 where 403 was written) together with executed evidence of the task's own changed code path (for example a test with a stubbed principal) is PASS with a limitation naming the defect; the refusal without that evidence is UNVERIFIED (missing coverage); goal not shown is BLOCKED. A positive criterion is never met by a refusal, and a literal form the requirement itself prescribes (a documented status-code contract) stays required. A fix of that foreign defect in the deliverable is not acceptance evidence; report it as out of scope ([out-of-scope discovery](../task-orchestrator/SKILL.md#out-of-scope-discovery)).

Judge actual test source and executed evidence for your criteria. Inspect any supplied current adequacy assessment. The gate separately checks pending sibling receipts. Report concrete test gaps. An omitted risk needs a category (a) [counterexample](../task-orchestrator/references/solution-design.md#2-triage-every-risk-only-required-risks-become-code). Counts and verdicts alone cannot prove behavior. AC cannot replace independent adequacy.

Use missing_coverage only for unmet proof required by this configured criterion at this gate. Any nonempty value blocks a mandatory criterion even if status says PASS. Put nonblocking coverage limits and mandatory later delivery inputs/effects in limitations and the pending delivery plan; they do not become prerequisites for current source approval. A real current evidence gap remains UNVERIFIED/BLOCKED. Passing a source criterion never establishes later publication or overall completion.

Apply task-orchestrator's [profile evidence](../task-orchestrator/references/profile-evidence.md). Software retains mandatory successful commands, positive actual test counts, no skipped required tests and current source/contract/plan fingerprints. Documents, research and infrastructure need substantive independent evaluation of their own deliverables. Suggest AC-derived checks independently of implementation assumptions.

Use `ase --project PROJECT verify TASK` through the authorized local backend adapter to capture independent receipts. A missing optional integration is not a prerequisite; unavailable independent-session capability is an explicit blocker. Do not manufacture receipts, copy credentials or relax permissions. Separate model judgment does not establish a separate OS security identity.

# Evidence, readiness and decisions

Use relevant sections for comparisons, blockers, dependencies, actionable artifacts, semantic changes or review findings. This refines the existing workflow; it adds no universal form, new approval or mandatory service. Clear authorized work proceeds. Use the [evidence brief](../assets/evidence-brief.md) when several material facts must stay aligned; otherwise retain them in existing notes.

## 1. Establish the target and reference

Identify the actual resource and relevant environment, tenant/account and consumer. For a comparison or migration, identify the reference's role and why it is authoritative for the requested result: an applicable owner decision, contract or verified provenance. Record its locator and current version. Deployed configuration proves what is used; availability, similar names and a colleague's implementation do not prove the right business baseline.

Separate inherited behavior/settings from changes introduced by this task. Reuse compatible project conventions; avoid an override solely because an inherited value differs from a guess. Investigate a material conflict with the approved target. Escalate an unresolved owner-only choice using the existing short question format. An unconfirmed reference does not authorize changing the target or unrelated systems.

## 2. Bound the claim and prove the blocker

A blocking claim names the required outcome, affected stage/dependents, and actual observation: operation, target, safe account/access-method reference, time/version, result and inspected scope. Keep credentials and raw responses out of notes. Distinguish a known failure from an unperformed check.

"Object not found in schema S with account A" is bounded evidence. "The object does not exist" needs corresponding coverage. One denied login or failed optional adapter does not prove the application is broken or all access is impossible. Try a concrete useful authorized alternative when available; an optional integration failure does not block usable CLI/file work. Do not request new access or change permissions silently.

Continue research while a specific lead can distinguish hypotheses. Stop on sufficient evidence, no useful lead, unavailable required access, an owner-only decision or an explicit stop/limit. Record the stopping reason and remaining unknowns; exhausted inspected sources are not absence everywhere. Then proceed with a supported in-scope choice or ask one material question: checked facts, unconfirmed hypothesis, recommendation/reason and decision needed. Hold affected work and continue independent approved work. Reconcile UNKNOWN external effects rather than replaying them.

A useful authorized alternative or a supported in-scope choice never includes fixing a defect outside the ticket that this task did not cause, even when it blocks your check: judge the criterion's goal under the conditions of [out-of-scope discovery](../SKILL.md#out-of-scope-discovery) and report the defect in one line.

## 3. Check the readiness the obligation actually needs

These are separate observations, not an automatic promotion ladder:

| Observation | What it establishes |
| --- | --- |
| Promised/announced | Delivery is unverified. |
| Exists/visible in metadata | The object/configuration is visible in the inspected scope. |
| Usable by intended account | The required authorized operation actually succeeds through the relevant access path. |
| Structurally complete | Required fields, interfaces and version are present. |
| Data suitable for this task | Bounded actual data/postconditions meet the task requirements. |
| Consumer behavior verified | A meaningful consumer-level check demonstrates required behavior. |

Record only the levels needed for the affected obligation, with evidence and unknowns. Installed tools are not usable sessions. Metadata is not a successful SELECT. Readable empty data is valid when the contract allows emptiness; it is not proof of representative data or correct calculations. Probe the relevant intended account/consumer within existing authority; do not broaden access or copy secrets. Once required postconditions are evidenced, proceed without a ceremonial checklist or new approval.

Bind required proof to the phase and action that can produce it. A current gate judges evidence causally attainable before its authorization; a criterion it judges must not require that same AC/review/gate approval or the later effects that approval authorizes. Independent AC/review and the current APPROVED gate remain mandatory authorization checks. If proof depends on the authorized action, retain that obligation as mandatory later work, leave its result pending, and verify it after the action before declaring the overall assignment complete.

Applying a migration, backfill or delete to shared or persistent data requires a backup, dry run on a copy and rollback plan, plus authorization for the exact target. Source preparation is separate.

If Publisher requires the whole-task gate, moving later proof to another stage of that same task does not remove the cycle. Scope its gated contract to source acceptance and retain the later mandatory obligations in an explicit publication/finish plan or separate delivery task. As applicable, these include actual publication, intended-consumer postconditions, matching remote/local SHA and dated closure. Source approval alone does not complete the overall assignment. Correcting this phase allocation within existing authorized scope needs no new approval; preserve every original obligation, independent verification and the gate, and never label future evidence PASS.

## 4. Separate artifact purpose, state and version

For an artifact that may be executed, handed off or used as evidence, retain:

- Purpose: discussion draft, reference/example, or intended execution/delivery.
- State: draft, prepared, applied/delivered, or independently verified, supported by actual evidence.
- Identity: path/object, content hash or meaningful version, target and relevant requirement/dependency source versions.
- Unresolved placeholders/assumptions and the current next action.

A reference CREATE script for an existing object is not a command to execute. Prepared text is not an applied resource. A filename such as final.sql is not readiness evidence. Before authorized execution or execution-ready handoff, inspect exact current bytes/version, target, required inputs and unresolved placeholders. A legitimate runtime parameter is not an unresolved placeholder. Check copied text for meaningful encoding/invisible-character corruption; do not strip whitespace or rewrite strings/identifiers blindly. Reuse authorization when its scope still applies; preparation/verification grants no external action by itself.

After a material answer or changed source, identify affected assumptions, artifact versions, acceptance checks and cached conclusions. Refresh these and their dependents, mark old versions historical/superseded, and update the current brief before the next action. Keep unaffected work valid and preserve evidence of already-applied effects; refreshing a draft does not authorize replay. Use existing intake/checkpoint/knowledge fields and source references. The brief is an optional view, not a new schema or second tracker.

## 5. Verify meaning when changing implementation

For migration, translation or optimization, identify required preserved behavior and its authority. Compare old/reference and proposed behavior using relevant examples: normal/boundary cases, null/missing values, duplicates, errors, ordering, rounding/units/time windows or permission effects as applicable. Use meaningful differential checks and the actual consumer contract. HTTP success, matching columns or one happy-path row alone do not prove equivalence.

A documented platform capability is a hypothesis about this execution path until checked. A narrowing filter needs evidence that excluded data cannot affect the required result. Separate a new regression from ambiguity already in the reference. Preserve supported behavior within scope; do not silently invent a business rule to resolve ambiguity. Hold only a material unresolved choice and its dependents, with a concise recommendation; continue independent work.

## 6. Substantiate and respond to review

Trace the current trigger through caller, boundary, callee, contract and observations; cite the first divergence/consequence. Missing code is a coverage gap to investigate, never a defect. Unknowns stay UNVERIFIED/BLOCKED.

For new software bugs use `--bugfix`. Distinguish symptom, cause and workaround. Justify the correction and new layers against the contract; preserve legitimate behavior. Use grounded consumer regressions with baseline/fault-injection evidence: helper-only green tests are insufficient. Continue useful authorized diagnostics before owner questions. See [bugfix procedure](bugfix-evidence.md) on demand.

Repair confirmed in-scope findings, rerun affected checks and fresh separate AC/review. Reject disproven findings with counterproof retained in history. Never speculate or downgrade P0/P1/P2 for approval. Preserve scope/recovery limits.

## 7. Wording and scope growth

Ambiguous wording read one way is an assumption. Declare new background, polling, global UI or shared-service changes in proposal `effects` before code ([procedure](scope-growth.md)); reviewers judge their necessity.

# Additional passes by the original main bot

After initial implementation and meaningful executed checks, the original main
chat must reconsider the whole solution `additional_passes` times for configured
nontrivial root tasks. Do not wait for the user to request edge cases. Workers
may investigate bounded questions; their reviews do not count as main-bot passes.
Independent acceptance, substantive review and software adequacy remain separate.

## Applicability and requirement authority

New CLI tasks get `additional_passes` 1 (LOW/MEDIUM risk) or 3 (HIGH).
Programmatic creators carry the explicit policy. Saved unconfigured contracts
stay historical; never fabricate old passes or silently rewrite their policy.
The requirement applies to final root completion in every supported domain.
Children/intermediate stages keep their own checks without another root barrier.

Default uncertain complexity to nontrivial. For genuinely mechanical LOW-risk
single-stage work, `lead-review classify` needs the concrete reason and current
passing checks/source. No actions, access, unresolved discovery/requirement gaps,
required children or mixed work. Reassess changed input. Independent AC must
explicitly agree with the exemption; a cheap implementation is not triviality.
Once a substantive critique is credited, the earlier mechanical classification
is historical: it cannot bypass recorded findings or the required review depth.

Every pass reads the original request and full approved contract/proposal
history from `prepare`. Include approved owner clarifications and label explicit
supersessions. Current code, implementation summaries and generated tests cannot
redefine expectations. Assess every mandatory criterion and original/latest
request using its provided requirement hash and concrete source/check evidence.

Each pass inspects the complete task. One pass covers all three focuses:

1. Requirements/business scenarios: omitted constraints, contradictions,
   unsupported assumptions and consistency with approved clarifications. For a bug,
   trace the reported actor, trigger, scope and expected result to the changed
   decision and executed evidence.
2. Attempts to break the result: boundaries, invalid inputs, dependency errors,
   repeated/concurrent effects, recovery, relevant security and performance.
   Performance conclusions need measurements. Justify inapplicable areas.
3. Whole-solution requirement reconciliation after fixes: interactions, actual
   consumer behavior, meaningful assertions and regression coverage. Check every
   original/current obligation again.

Every pass also sweeps the whole diff for domain conversions and magic values
(date/code formats, units, external-system numbers or keys, unexplained
literals): each one uses an existing helper or constant, goes into the existing
helper class of its domain as a method or named constant, or becomes a named
constant with a reason. Code that is correct is not exempt.

For software, read the final diff as the developer who will explain it. Check whether each
nontrivial rule belongs in the chosen class, whether a maintained neighbor already handles it
and whether names and control flow fit the project. Trace material contract changes to callers,
including callers outside the ticket's immediate path. Check actual dependency and deployment
files against the approved decisions. For an integration removal, verify remaining references
in configuration, deployment and docs. For a boundary mapping, compare the actual producer and
consumer contract and any compatible examples inspected within scope. Check original producer
output and the affected consumers before accepting a workaround. Check the rationale in the PR
draft for nonobvious public signature changes.
If an in-scope repair needs a material decision outside the plan, get approval before editing.
Report unrelated defects, including ones that block a check, through
[out-of-scope discovery](../SKILL.md#out-of-scope-discovery). Preserve the owner of an approved
deferred obligation in the handoff.

Zero findings is legitimate. A finding identifies a requirement, concrete
violation/counterexample, source and executed evidence. Investigate suspicions;
do not mutate for speculative defects, preferences or invented requirements. A
newly found risk without a category (a) counterexample ([risk triage](solution-design.md#2-triage-every-risk-only-required-risks-become-code))
goes under "Not handled".
Where useful, check that tests detect a relevant deliberately broken behavior;
passing counts alone do not establish fault detection.

**Record the assessment before fixes.** Repair confirmed in-scope findings under
existing authority, rerun affected checks/regressions, then perform the next
pass on current facts. If input changed before capture, retain the original
response as stale, settle its ticket and prepare a current critique. Earlier
valid passes survive later fixes, but the final critique must be current. A fix
after the last pass requires a corrective follow-up. Explicitly resolve earlier
finding IDs; omitting them cannot close them.

A new approved requirement anchor starts its own pass depth. It does not
close old material findings, even when a criterion is renamed or removed. The
host replays authenticated prior series, including old databases without carry
fields. `prepare.finding_ledger` identifies each finding's original anchor.
New response schemas require `origin_anchor_sha256` in resolutions: use an empty
string for this series or the exact inherited origin for an older finding.
IDs may be reused in another series without conflating their obligations.
Legacy responses remain local to their original series. A `fixed` disposition
needs changed evidence; `not_a_bug` needs counterproof under the original rule
or a concrete explicit saved owner-approved supersession, challenged by AC.
Old open findings also block a later trivial exemption. Original inputs for
inherited obligations remain available beside current passes; old passes never
count toward current depth. Missing/tampered credited history blocks completion.

Pass depth is initial checking depth, not a guarantee or a repair cap. Continue for
material gaps under existing progress-sensitive recovery. Three unsuccessful
repair cycles without verified progress trigger reassessment; another review
paragraph is not progress. Ask only for a genuine remaining decision/access/scope
blocker. Routine fixes of defects inside the approved task scope or caused by this
task's changes, and further supported checks, do not need another approval; any
other defect is reported, never fixed ([out-of-scope discovery](../SKILL.md#out-of-scope-discovery)).

## Reading earlier passes in a packet

Each pass's `inputs` in `_ase_context/lead_review.json` names its `packet_path`:
an identical current file or `_ase_lead_history/<hash>.txt`. Compare earlier
findings with those original inputs and with the current corrections. A
`line_delta_v1` reference names a JSON recipe over a complete current base file
in the same packet (`base_packet_path`): split the base with
`splitlines(keepends=True)` (`line_delta_v2` first normalises CRLF to LF), copy
base lines before each `start`, append its `content`, skip base lines up to
`until` (exclusive), then append the rest; indexes refer to the original base. A `$ref` contract points to the identical
`_ase_context/contract.json`; a `/scope` reference may list `exclude_resources`
to drop from the current order. The host has already checked every hash, size and
range before the packet was built, so do not claim to have recomputed hashes;
reconstruct read-only and never treat it as an edit. Missing, tampered or
oversized history is listed as missing coverage and prevents verified completion.
A URL the owner supplied is scope, not proof of observed state; remote checks are
proven by the captured log named in `check_sources`. Do not ask the owner to rebuild
retrievable local evidence or drop an earlier finding to obtain approval. Stage packets avoid the final-root barrier.

The original main bot's commands, recovery and sealing rules are in
[lead-review CLI](lead-review-cli.md).

# Profile evidence

Select a profile by the requested action. A finance report's data warnings are not software debugging; changing the generating code is software. Mixed tasks map every obligation to stages and child tasks without weakening parent coverage.

Apply the [readiness proof boundary](evidence-decisions.md#3-check-the-readiness-the-obligation-actually-needs) when allocating profile evidence. Current acceptance uses proof causally attainable before its gate; later authorized effects remain mandatory in the publication/finish plan or delivery task and pending until checked. A whole-task publication gate includes all its stages, so stage reassignment alone cannot separate future proof. Phase-local source approval does not establish publication, postconditions or overall completion.

| Profile | Evidence to collect |
| --- | --- |
| software | Executed mandatory commands, positive test counts, no skipped required tests, independent AC and code review, current source/contract/plan fingerprints |
| infrastructure | Actual resource identity, before/after observations, operation intent and reconciliation, independent postcondition evidence; no invented resource success |
| document | Required artifact, readable rendering/structure where applicable, required content and traceable sources, independent acceptance and substantive review |
| research | Sources and dates, claim-to-source coverage, clear inference and uncertainty, independent acceptance and substantive review |
| mixed | Required parent coverage across all child profiles and stages; no completed parent while mandatory children remain unresolved |

Configured evaluators determine executed facts; model judgments remain separate. `manual` evidence has no recording command and cannot pass; use an artifact, test, command or probe evidence kind with its source instead. A protocol test establishes the protocol only. Missing mandatory resources or independent execution remain BLOCKED. Local reliability records do not enforce publishing against another process with the same OS identity; trusted CI and server rules are required for that boundary.

A documented platform capability is a hypothesis about this execution path until checked. A narrowing filter needs evidence that excluded data cannot affect the required result. Separate a new regression from ambiguity already in the reference. Preserve supported behavior within scope; do not silently invent a business rule to resolve ambiguity. Hold only a material unresolved choice and its dependents, with a concise recommendation; continue independent work.

## 6. Substantiate and respond to review

Trace the current trigger through caller, boundary, callee, contract and observations; cite the first divergence/consequence. Missing code is a coverage gap to investigate, never a defect. Unknowns stay UNVERIFIED/BLOCKED.

For new software bugs use `--bugfix`. Distinguish symptom, cause and workaround. Justify the correction and new layers against the contract; preserve legitimate behavior. Use grounded consumer regressions with baseline/fault-injection evidence: helper-only green tests are insufficient. Continue useful authorized diagnostics before owner questions. See [bugfix procedure](bugfix-evidence.md) on demand.

Repair confirmed in-scope findings, rerun affected checks and fresh separate AC/review. Reject disproven findings with counterproof retained in history. Never speculate or downgrade P0/P1/P2 for approval. Preserve scope/recovery limits.

## 7. Wording and scope growth

Ambiguous wording read one way is an assumption. Declare new background, polling, global UI or shared-service changes in proposal `effects` before code ([procedure](scope-growth.md)); reviewers judge their necessity.

# Additional passes by the original main bot

After initial implementation and meaningful executed checks, the original main
chat must reconsider the whole solution `additional_passes` times for configured
nontrivial root tasks. Do not wait for the user to request edge cases. Workers
may investigate bounded questions; their reviews do not count as main-bot passes.
Independent acceptance, substantive review and software adequacy remain separate.

## Applicability and requirement authority

New CLI tasks get `additional_passes` 1 (LOW/MEDIUM risk) or 3 (HIGH).
Programmatic creators carry the explicit policy. Saved unconfigured contracts
stay historical; never fabricate old passes or silently rewrite their policy.
The requirement applies to final root completion in every supported domain.
Children/intermediate stages keep their own checks without another root barrier.

Default uncertain complexity to nontrivial. For genuinely mechanical LOW-risk
single-stage work, `lead-review classify` needs the concrete reason and current
passing checks/source. No actions, access, unresolved discovery/requirement gaps,
required children or mixed work. Reassess changed input. Independent AC must
explicitly agree with the exemption; a cheap implementation is not triviality.
Once a substantive critique is credited, the earlier mechanical classification
is historical: it cannot bypass recorded findings or the required review depth.

Every pass reads the original request and full approved contract/proposal
history from `prepare`. Include approved owner clarifications and label explicit
supersessions. Current code, implementation summaries and generated tests cannot
redefine expectations. Assess every mandatory criterion and original/latest
request using its provided requirement hash and concrete source/check evidence.
Missing relevant facts are UNVERIFIED, not invented business policies or bugs.

## Pass focuses

Each pass inspects the complete task. One pass covers all three focuses:

1. Requirements/business scenarios: omitted constraints, contradictions,
   unsupported assumptions and consistency with approved clarifications. For a bug,
   trace the reported actor, trigger, scope and expected result to the changed
   decision and executed evidence.
2. Attempts to break the result: boundaries, invalid inputs, dependency errors,
   repeated/concurrent effects, recovery, relevant security and performance.
   Performance conclusions need measurements. Justify inapplicable areas.
3. Whole-solution requirement reconciliation after fixes: interactions, actual
   consumer behavior, meaningful assertions and regression coverage. Check every
   original/current obligation again.

Every pass also sweeps the whole diff for domain conversions and magic values
(date/code formats, units, external-system numbers or keys, unexplained
literals): each one uses an existing helper or constant, goes into the existing
helper class of its domain as a method or named constant, or becomes a named
constant with a reason. Code that is correct is not exempt.

For software, read the final diff as the developer who will explain it. Check whether each
nontrivial rule belongs in the chosen class, whether a maintained neighbor already handles it
and whether names and control flow fit the project. Trace material contract changes to callers,
including callers outside the ticket's immediate path. Check actual dependency and deployment
files against the approved decisions. For an integration removal, verify remaining references
in configuration, deployment and docs. For a boundary mapping, compare the actual producer and
consumer contract and any compatible examples inspected within scope. Check original producer
output and the affected consumers before accepting a workaround. Check the rationale in the PR
draft for nonobvious public signature changes.
If an in-scope repair needs a material decision outside the plan, get approval before editing.
Report unrelated defects, including ones that block a check, through
[out-of-scope discovery](../SKILL.md#out-of-scope-discovery). Preserve the owner of an approved
deferred obligation in the handoff.

Zero findings is legitimate. A finding identifies a requirement, concrete
violation/counterexample, source and executed evidence. Investigate suspicions;
do not mutate for speculative defects, preferences or invented requirements. A
newly found risk without a category (a) counterexample ([risk triage](solution-design.md#2-triage-every-risk-only-required-risks-become-code))
goes under "Not handled".
Where useful, check that tests detect a relevant deliberately broken behavior;
passing counts alone do not establish fault detection.

**Record the assessment before fixes.** Repair confirmed in-scope findings under
existing authority, rerun affected checks/regressions, then perform the next
pass on current facts. If input changed before capture, retain the original
response as stale, settle its ticket and prepare a current critique. Earlier
valid passes survive later fixes, but the final critique must be current. A fix
after the last pass requires a corrective follow-up. Explicitly resolve earlier
finding IDs; omitting them cannot close them.

A new approved requirement anchor starts its own pass depth. It does not
close old material findings, even when a criterion is renamed or removed. The
host replays authenticated prior series, including old databases without carry
fields. `prepare.finding_ledger` identifies each finding's original anchor.
New response schemas require `origin_anchor_sha256` in resolutions: use an empty
string for this series or the exact inherited origin for an older finding.
IDs may be reused in another series without conflating their obligations.
Legacy responses remain local to their original series. A `fixed` disposition
needs changed evidence; `not_a_bug` needs counterproof under the original rule
or a concrete explicit saved owner-approved supersession, challenged by AC.
Old open findings also block a later trivial exemption. Original inputs for
inherited obligations remain available beside current passes; old passes never
count toward current depth. Missing/tampered credited history blocks completion.

Pass depth is initial checking depth, not a guarantee or a repair cap. Continue for
material gaps under existing progress-sensitive recovery. Three unsuccessful
repair cycles without verified progress trigger reassessment; another review
paragraph is not progress. Ask only for a genuine remaining decision/access/scope
blocker. Routine fixes of defects inside the approved task scope or caused by this
task's changes, and further supported checks, do not need another approval; any
other defect is reported, never fixed ([out-of-scope discovery](../SKILL.md#out-of-scope-discovery)).

## Reading earlier passes in a packet

Each pass's `inputs` in `_ase_context/lead_review.json` names its `packet_path`:
an identical current file or `_ase_lead_history/<hash>.txt`. Compare earlier
findings with those original inputs and with the current corrections. A
`line_delta_v1` reference names a JSON recipe over a complete current base file
in the same packet (`base_packet_path`): split the base with
`splitlines(keepends=True)` (`line_delta_v2` first normalises CRLF to LF), copy
base lines before each `start`, append its `content`, skip base lines up to
`until` (exclusive), then append the rest; indexes refer to the original base. A `$ref` contract points to the identical
`_ase_context/contract.json`; a `/scope` reference may list `exclude_resources`
to drop from the current order. The host has already checked every hash, size and
range before the packet was built, so do not claim to have recomputed hashes;
reconstruct read-only and never treat it as an edit. Missing, tampered or
oversized history is listed as missing coverage and prevents verified completion.
A URL the owner supplied is scope, not proof of observed state; remote checks are
proven by the captured log named in `check_sources`. Do not ask the owner to rebuild
retrievable local evidence or drop an earlier finding to obtain approval. Stage packets avoid the final-root barrier.

The original main bot's commands, recovery and sealing rules are in
[lead-review CLI](lead-review-cli.md).

# Proportionate solution design

Use before choosing how to implement a software or infrastructure change. Build the smallest
change that meets the ticket's acceptance criteria and fits the project's existing patterns, the
way a careful developer on this team would. Correct code with unrequested machinery is a failed
delivery: the team has to remove it. A workaround that avoids touching the right code is not
"small" either. Scale the steps below to the task: one line each for a trivial change. See the
[calibration examples](solution-calibration.md).

## 0. Understand the problem first; code comes after

The first deliverable is a short problem analysis, before any code:

- **What happens now**, reproduced or traced in the code: the actual flow and data.
- **Where the system already meets the condition**: the existing point that detects or handles
  it (the place where using a token fails, the status transition, the query that selects items).
- **The smallest hook point** for the change.
- **The ticket class**: code change, investigation/clarification, or both.
- **For a defect**, its scope: every entry point with the same root cause and any earlier
  compensations for it.

For a bug, first check that the behaviour is really a defect. When it is a question of
expectations (rows that differ by version, data the reporter misread), the deliverable is a
finding for the owner and, when needed, a draft question for the reporter. Compare the original
example or attachment with the actual behavior before deciding. When ticket text and a later
clarification differ, identify the approving source, the scope of this delivery and who owns the
remaining obligation. Write no code until the analysis exists and matches the authorized scope.
When a host request includes `handoff.task_proposal.ancestor_proposals`, use each saved plan
for its named ancestor stage and apply its relevant decisions within the child task scope.

## 1. Understand the system before deciding

- **Business need.** Restate what the requester needs to happen, not only the wording.
- **Bug scenario.** Before editing, pin down the actor or caller, exact operation and trigger, the
  scope of the rule, what actually happens and what should happen. Check the original ticket,
  examples and approved clarifications. Two operations using the same integration can have
  different settings, permissions and events. If the expected result still depends on a product
  decision, present the smallest distinguishing example to the owner before implementing that
  behavior. A failing test, trace or concrete reproduction should cover the reported path.
  Record limitations when that evidence is unavailable.
- **Scoped system map** (C4, only the part the change touches): dependent apps/users;
  services/apps, how they exchange data and **who owns each contract**; components and the
  existing path for this kind of work; the files to change and their size. Use code, config,
  docs/ADRs, Git history and PR/issue discussion; mark what is unverified.
- **Reuse first.** Before adding any mechanism, search for the project's existing one
  (email/notification command, job, transaction pattern, validation, caching, auth check) and use
  it. Record what you searched and found. Adding a case at the project's existing extension point
  (an exception-to-response mapping, a registry, a switch over types) is reuse, not a shared-service
  change; a restriction on named shared components applies only to those components. When unsure,
  offer it to the owner as a plan option; never build a parallel copy. The norm is the project's own
  maintained code near the change: new code in an existing file follows its siblings' conventions,
  wraps an existing API in error handling only as its other callers do, and parses an external API
  the way the project already parses it. Extra defensive code needs a concrete trigger on the base
  branch; code whose only effect is in another, unmerged change does not belong here. Keep the base
  structure of a changed method: no pre-declared locals or re-indented unchanged code only to fit new
  control flow.
- **Before and while coding.**
  - *Remove and see.* For every new catch, guard, fallback, conversion or check, state what breaks on
    the base branch if it is removed. If nothing breaks, do not add it.
  - *Proportional diff.* Before coding, estimate the change size from the requirement. If the actual
    diff grows clearly larger, stop and explain the difference in the plan instead of continuing.
  - *Ask before working around.* If the simplest correct change touches code a rule or instruction
    seems to protect, stop and ask the owner with both options; never build a parallel mechanism to
    avoid the question.
  - *Shared files in a task set.* When several branches or PRs of one task set change the same file,
    detect it early (for example `git merge-tree` between the open branches), name one branch as the
    owner of that file's change and ask the owner for the merge order before both are finished.
  - *Readable classifications.* Write a classification as an explicit named set with one case per line;
    never introduce a constant to bound an impossible value. Keep exception and model types plain
    unless the project's own precedent puts logic there.
  - *Existing tooling first.* When the project configures analyzers, linters or formatters, run them
    on the changed files and declare that run as an evidence check so its output reaches the
    reviewers. Never install or configure new tools.
- **Precedent.** Follow the team's established way unless evidence shows it no longer fits. An
  explicit example-search opt-out skips deliberate example search while preserving inspection of
  actual callers and dependencies. On a
  codebase new to you or the team, match the existing code style and change size over general best
  practice, and apply this guide strictly.
- **Code placement.** For nontrivial logic, inspect the existing owner of the rule and one nearby
  caller or maintained equivalent. Compare reusing the existing method, extending its owner and
  keeping the change local. Extend a class when the behavior belongs to its responsibility and its
  callers can share the same contract. Similar code alone is insufficient reason to create a shared
  helper or dependency. Follow applicable project conventions and nearby maintained code. Choose
  clear names and control flow the team can read without chasing unnecessary wrappers or branches.
  Keep a related refactor within the changed flow and check the affected callers.
- **Types of a recognisable kind.** Before creating a new exception, DTO or model, enum,
  constants holder, extension or helper class, mapper, validator or interface, search where the
  project keeps existing types of that kind (same base type, suffix or role) and follow the
  majority folder and namespace. When several homes exist, follow the closest siblings: same
  layer and same role (for example exceptions the web layer maps to HTTP responses). The new
  type's first consumer does not decide its home; an example of the behavior is not an example
  of where that kind lives. A different placement needs a one-line reason in the technical plan.
- **Review evidence.** In the technical plan name the existing path, the chosen class or method,
  the relevant precedent and why the change belongs there. If the search finds no suitable
  precedent, record where you looked. Include the few unchanged source files decisive to the review
  as read-only discovery dependencies. Examples include the existing owner of the behavior, an
  affected caller, or the applicable project rule. Keep the mutation scope limited to the task.
  Include the relevant test locations in the edit scope when the task needs new regression proof.
  For a shared contract, name the callers and the behavior they rely on.
- **Root cause.** For wrong or missing data, trace caller -> boundary -> callee to the first place
  the value becomes wrong. Read the callee's implementation and its sibling paths over the same
  data; an existing handling of the same condition there (fallback to the primary store,
  consistency check) is the first candidate fix. Record what you searched in the callee.

## 2. Triage every risk; only required risks become code

For each risk scenario you can think of (race, transient failure, stale data, duplicates,
concurrent edits), classify it:

- **(a) Required** -> code and test it. A risk is required when:
  - the ticket or an acceptance criterion asks for it, or a reviewer demonstrates the concrete
    counterexample below; or
  - without it, the change itself would break the project's existing authorization, validation
    or error conventions on new paths, existing invariants and contracts, lose or corrupt data,
    or duplicate external or financial effects (with a concrete counterexample).
- **(b) Already handled** by existing behaviour (a one-time state transition, an existing
  transaction, a later re-check) -> note where.
- **(c) Unlikely or out of scope** -> do not code it; list it under "Not handled" in the PR with
  the reason ("not required by AC-x; no observed trigger").

"More robust" is not a requirement. A theoretical race is (c) unless the ticket or evidence makes
it real. A risk found later (review, lead pass, adequacy check) follows the same triage: without an
(a) counterexample it goes under "Not handled", not into code or tests.

**Hold edits that depend on an unresolved decision.** Follow the proposed failure path through
the caller response and any committed write or external effect. A failure after a write can be a
new regression even when the same pattern is used elsewhere. If the known contract settles the
failure behavior, use it. If the acceptable result after failure needs an owner decision, show
what is saved, what is missing and what a replay can do, then present conditional options.
Keep independently approved edits moving. An open owner question about the behavior is never
approval of a patch that already chooses it.

## 3. Hook into existing flows; mechanisms need a reason

Prefer the place where the system already encounters the condition. Add no new scheduled job,
trigger, pipeline, polling, or global/root UI component (app shell, root component, global
layout) unless the ticket explicitly requires it.
For proposed background work, separate the schedule from delivery guarantees. Check the actual
platform contract and deployment configuration for relevant replica count, retries and overlap.
If those facts are unavailable, state them as conditions on the recommendation. A time trigger
alone establishes no guarantee that a job will complete exactly once.
For changed handler registration, invocation or result handling, run a check through the actual
dispatcher and observe the durable state or consumer result. Check the arguments passed to the
handler and what consumes its output. A local fixture may replace external infrastructure while
keeping the application dispatch path intact.

Locks (local or distributed), new or conditional transactions, atomic claims, retries, timeouts or
waits, queues, caches, polling, version/incident IDs, new columns/tables/migrations, and optional or nullable DI
dependencies are added only when:

- a category (a) risk needs them,
- a documented contract prescribes them for that flow (for example a published transient-error
  retry policy for idempotent calls; use the shared implementation), or
- the project already uses that exact mechanism for that exact flow.

This applies to recommended options and interim "quick fixes" as well as code.

Otherwise leave the risk documented and unhandled, or ask the owner. Do not wrap new code in
defensive re-checks of state the existing code already guarantees.

Whether an addition beyond the ticket is "really needed" is not your call. Keep it only as an
explicit question to the developer or lead, with its reason; never keep it silently.

## 4. Fix at the source, for every consumer

For a persisted key or wire-format correction, verify existing records and old callers as well
as new writes. For affected response fields, cover omission, null, false and zero where the
contract gives them distinct meanings.
When reusing shared logic that requires new fields or values, exercise older valid inputs at the
changed entry point, including supported records with missing fields or retired values.

- Before changing a service boundary format, check the current producer and consumer contract.
  Compare maintained neighbors using that contract when example search is allowed. Preserve
  established wire values, units, casing and absence semantics. If there is a material
  conflict, cite the evidence and ask the contract owner. Include the decisive contract or
  unchanged caller in review.
- When removing an integration, search for the service and provider names, registration symbols,
  configuration and environment keys, and endpoint aliases. Check code, settings for each
  environment, deployment files and docs. Remove obsolete references owned by the removal and
  explain any live shared references that remain. Give review the searched locations and results.
  Record key names and paths while keeping secret values out of evidence.

- Fix the component that produces the wrong value. Compare the real output at the boundary to the
  agreed contract and check callers, existing compensations and downstream effects. A compatible
  repair in approved scope can proceed at the source, including in shared code. Declare a shared
  change and its affected consumers. When the correction has broad downstream impact, consumers
  may rely on the bad output, or you cannot establish a safe boundary, show the owner what can
  change and ask them to decide how to proceed before editing the affected flow.
- Code in another repository (another team's service) is changed through its own managed task or
  child task, with its own baseline, gate, review and publication authorization. Prepare that
  change; the other team's code review is not an owner approval and does not hold your work.
  Their ownership alone does not justify a consumer-side workaround.
- A consumer-side workaround (mapper, fallback, re-computation, retry, wait, cache) needs a
  documented requirement or contract, or the owner's explicit approval when the source cannot
  be changed. Put temporary workarounds at the integration boundary and record the upstream
  reference and removal condition. Data the source accepted but does not yet return (replica
  lag, stale read) is a source fault unless the source's documented contract allows that lag.
- When valid and invalid responses overlap, try the same observed input under both
  interpretations. Show the different outcomes if the data cannot distinguish them. A
  plausible number is insufficient evidence for a workaround
  affecting a charge, permission, or persisted record. If the contract gives no reliable
  signal or authorized fallback, present the ambiguous example and choices, then wait for
  the owner's decision before implementing a rule that changes outcomes.
- Fix or remove existing compensations only when the approved repair needs that change. Record
  the remaining consumer impact for the owner.
- When the same fault of the ticket's defect exists at several entry points, fix every one in this change. Use a shared
  handler/mapping when one already exists for that purpose; otherwise apply the same small fix at
  each entry point and offer the shared version as a separate ticket. These hunks belong to the
  defect, not to "unrelated changes".

## 5. Choose a proportionate form

State the chosen form, why not simpler and why not more complex.

| Situation | Proportionate form | Wrong in either direction |
|---|---|---|
| A few lines in a large file | Edit those lines; tidy only the touched code when the risk is low or medium | Restructuring the file "while here" |
| Substantial new logic for a large file | New classes/files (folder, or a project in the solution when large), called from the existing code | Growing the large file further |
| The task changes most of a component's logic | Restructure that part, tests first, risk stated | Patching around it |
| The ticket says how to do it ("do not refactor") | Follow it; note any risk | Overriding the instruction |
| Data available through one simple join/navigation | Read it there | A duplicate column |
| Data required by the ticket and not stored anywhere | A new column, approved by the owner (see 6) | Heuristics, log parsing, heavy procedures |
| A new entity with its own lifecycle | A new table (infrastructure, see 6) | Overloading unrelated tables |
| A monolith needs a capability | A module/project in the solution, reusing existing services | A new service, function or queue |
| Several services need a capability none provides | A dedicated component/service (infrastructure, see 6) | Copying it into each service |
| A policy value changes | Change the value and its test | Config systems, date switches, flags |

## 6. Who decides

- **You decide** (justify in the proposal): code in any number of services in this workspace, new
  files/folders/projects inside a solution, refactoring whose risk you judge low or medium in the
  task's code or the flows it tests, additions that follow a pattern the service already uses,
  root-cause fixes in shared code, `kind: "schema"` changes - an index or constraint migration a
  requirement needs. Identify affected consumers of shared code and preserve behavior their
  contracts require. Routine decisions remain within the approved change.
- **In the implementation plan for the owner** (task-orchestrator, Plan and approval): HIGH -
  every item in the list below, including a new table or column and replacing a technology;
  MEDIUM - a new direct third-party dependency or direct dependency on a shared library in the
  affected service, a material architecture change (for example the first Unit of Work), or a
  material change to shared behavior or a cross-service contract. An externally consumed message
  type on an existing queue is a contract decision. LOW is risky or
  complex refactoring required by the task. A pattern used only in a sibling service can be a
  precedent and still be a material change in the target. Give the reason, the simplest existing
  alternative, the concrete gap it leaves, the affected consumers and your recommendation.
  A general go-ahead covers routine choices. For HIGH or MEDIUM changes, present the rationale
  before editing. The owner's reply to a plan they saw can cover the named change. Prior
  authorization must name the change or a bounded delegated choice in the owner's own words.
  Recording a self-authored plan under general pre-approval does not supply that authority.
- **Incidental shared-code changes** - hardening, claim logic or other edits to job runners,
  schedulers, publishers, DB context, DI setup or middleware that the root cause does not need -
  stay out of a feature ticket. Paths listed in `.devframework/protected-paths.txt` additionally
  block the gate until `ase authorize-protected` records the owner's permission; ask for it in the
  approval format below and build no workaround meanwhile.
- **The owner approves before you build** any added or removed infrastructure (`kind:
  "infrastructure"`):
  - a service or application;
  - a column, and replacing a technology (message broker, database engine);
  - a database or a table;
  - an Azure Function or other serverless unit;
  - any timer, scheduler or background job, including an in-process hosted service;
  - a queue, topic or subscription;
  - an external platform or provider;
  - a new cloud resource.

  DB functions, procedures and triggers count as infrastructure unless the project already uses
  them for that kind of logic. Declare each with basis `ASSUMPTION` on a blocking unknown; only the
  owner's answer resolves it, never a retrievable fact (`DECISION` once answered). A source ref
  counts only when the owner's own text names that infrastructure and covers the intended action.
  The CLI checks the binding and reviewers check what the owner actually authorized.
  Under pre-approval the owner can authorize preparing infrastructure files in the pull request
  and explicitly allow a dev environment for application. Record the message as the
  `resolution`, marked pre-approved, with the environment and authorized action.
- **The approval request** (in the implementation plan it is the HIGH item, not a separate message) gives:
  - the business need and the evidence;
  - the options from simplest up (for example lazy expiry on access, an existing job, sending from
    each service), and why each is or is not enough;
  - the recommendation and its impact on other services, operations and cost;
  - one decision to make.
- **Do not ask** about what code, docs or history answer, internal design choices, which team
  reviews code, or release timing for a change you can prepare now. When the ticket implies a date
  ("from next month"), state the date you read and proceed; put it in the release note instead of
  holding the change.

## 7. Developer ownership and human-led mode

- Give the developer a short walkthrough of the original behavior, why this location is the
  right hook, the observed result of the relevant check and any material remaining obligation.
  The PR description should let a teammate understand the decision and its verification.
- **Human-led mode** is on only when the task explicitly asks for it, or when AGENTS.md contains the
  exact line `DevelopmentFramework mode: human-led` (then for the whole project). Nothing else
  enables it. In this mode the developer writes the production code. DF:
  - gives the analysis, hook point, step plan and test proposals;
  - writes tests only on request;
  - independently reviews the developer's diff and polishes text.

  The task runs under the research/review profile, without an implementation gate.

## 8. One ticket, proportionate tests, plain PR

- One ticket per PR. A defect outside the ticket found on the way is reported in one line ("Found
  separate defect X (evidence); outside this ticket, left untouched. Open a separate task?"), with no
  fix, branch or PR, current or separate ([out-of-scope discovery](../SKILL.md#out-of-scope-discovery)).
- Tests cover the acceptance criteria and category (a) risks, written, not promised; prove the
  original failure through the real consumer path where practical.
- Where tests go follows what the project already has. When an existing test project covers the
  changed layer, add the tests there and publish them with the change. When the project has no
  tests, or none for the changed layer, still write and run the tests the task needs, but keep them
  local: never stage, commit, push or put them in a PR, and say so in one report line ("tests run
  locally, not added: the project has no tests for this layer"). Adding a test project or test
  infrastructure is the owner's decision; where the project has tests elsewhere, ask in one line
  whether to add them. Local tests remain the task's executed evidence and adequacy proof.
  No tests for invented races, and no test volume several times larger than the change.
- Required side effects (messages, payments) avoid duplicates on retry and keep related writes in
  one existing transaction where the context allows (an instance of 2(a)). Prefer a reliable signal
  over a heuristic.
- PR description: short and plain - what the ticket asked, what changed, what was deliberately not
  handled, how it was verified. No showcase of mechanisms.
- For a nonobvious public signature change, add one sentence on why the caller needs the new
  contract and check affected callers. Put the reason in the proposal summary so it reaches
  pre-publication review, and retain it in the PR description. Example reason given to reviewers
  would be that the caller needs the assigned identifier without a second read.

Independent review checks proportionality as a blocking criterion: unrequired mechanisms,
incidental shared-code edits, bundled unrelated changes, avoidable workarounds and unapproved
infrastructure are findings. A diff far larger than the minimal sketch triggers that scrutiny; the
finding names the specific unrequired hunks.

# Solution calibration examples

Real tickets where correct but over-engineered changes were rejected by the team lead
("I hired a person, not an AI agent"), and the proportional solution. Use them to judge
size and mechanisms; they are not templates.

## 1. Integration lost authorization: email admins, show a banner with a reconnect link

- **Over-engineered (31 files, +545 lines):**
  - atomic "claim job" logic in the shared background-job runner, affecting every job;
  - distributed locks around connect, disconnect and email sending;
  - a custom deferred email queue with retries and stale-email cancellation, although the
    project already had a standard send-email command;
  - a per-incident ID plus a migration to deduplicate emails;
  - a token re-check inside code that already held a lock;
  - a banner that polled the server every minute.
- **Proportional:** send the email through the existing command when the integration status
  changes from Active to Broken. Verify the existing transition prevents repeat alerts on a
  subsequent call. If the approved scope includes a banner, use the existing feature area. If
  the owner limits this delivery to email, record the clarification and who owns the UI work.

## 2. "Don't sync private items to the external system"

- **Over-engineered:**
  - the filter, plus a project-wide distributed lock between "edit visibility" and "sync";
  - a conditional transaction (`tx = locked ? null : BeginTransaction()`);
  - an optional constructor dependency (`ILock lock = null` plus a null guard);
  - re-reads under the lock and two extra visibility re-checks;
  - unrelated behaviour changes.
- **Proportional when visibility is defined at batch selection:** one query filter excluding
  private items, plus tests for it. If the requirement instead covers changes committed before
  upload starts, the snapshot-only filter misses that criterion. Use the established, applicable
  timing contract when the ticket leaves it implicit. Ask the owner only if the timing remains
  materially ambiguous after checking authoritative sources and changes the decision.

## 3. "Allow downloads only from the project's workspace; return 403 for others"

- **Over-engineered:** the correct check, plus:
  - a 10-minute cache with hashed keys that duplicated a re-check already done on download;
  - an unrelated auth bug fix bundled into the same PR.
- **Proportional:** the workspace check returning 403, plus tests. The unrelated auth bug is
  reported in one line ("Found separate defect X (evidence); outside this ticket, left untouched.
  Open a separate task?"), with no fix, branch or PR, current or separate
  ([out-of-scope discovery](../SKILL.md#out-of-scope-discovery)).

## 4. "Duplicates in the sync log export" (a bug ticket that was a question)

- **Wrong:** went straight to a code change.
- **Right:**
  - the rows differed by version, so the expected behaviour was already in place;
  - explain the difference to the owner and draft a question to the reporter if the desired
    display remains unclear.

## 5. "Email admins when auth lapses" (a new pipeline instead of the existing point)

- **Wrong:**
  - invented a scheduled validation job, which is a new pipeline;
  - changed the root app component to show a banner, although the lead said that component must
    not be touched;
  - a "simplified" version kept both, because the agent judged them "really needed" without asking.
- **Right:** send the email at the existing point where using the token fails. Clarify the scope
  if the ticket still lists a UI alert and the lead's decision covers email only.

## 6. "Use the server's permissions for the project settings card"

The adjacent settings card derives `CanEdit` from the same role rule as its write commands.
The feature owner confirms that a user arriving through the organization view retains edit
rights when also a project captain.

- **Wrong:** add another frontend permissions helper or copy the server's role logic into the
  component. The UI can again disagree with the write commands.
- **Right:** compute the flag from the existing project permission rule and read it in the card.
  Verify a captain, a view-only user and a user with both roles. Check that the banner describes
  the agreed behavior. Supply the adjacent settings query and the write guards as review inputs.

## 7. "Explain why connecting a project failed"

The current connect path and a background sync both call a shared session service. Changing it
from throwing an error to returning an empty result can send the background caller down a
different path even if the connect UI shows the expected message.

- **Right:** inspect both callers. Prefer the existing error mapping if it can carry the message.
  If the shared contract must change, show the owner the effect on both flows in the plan and
  verify each. The review needs the unchanged background caller to judge the effect.

## 8. "Schedule a daily reminder"

A sibling service uses a package for scheduling. The target service already has a queue and a
worker but no scheduling package or timer deployment. The owner has given a general go-ahead.

- **Wrong:** add the sibling package or deploy a new timer on the assumption that a nearby
  precedent or the general go-ahead supplies approval.
- **Right:** first check whether the existing worker has a suitable trigger. If a new package or
  timer is needed, name it and explain the gap and affected deployment before editing. Approval
  of a plan naming that decision covers it. An ordinary handler using a trigger already established
  in the target service remains a routine implementation choice.

## 9. "Remove the legacy carrier client"

Search the client name and configuration keys across all environment settings, registrations,
deployment and docs. An unchanged production override can still point to the deleted client.
Remove obsolete references in scope and give the reviewer the matching paths or search result.

## 10. "Send the site type to the destination service"

The peer producer sends the canonical site codes verbatim. Confirm that both integrations
use the same contract and forward those values. If an incoming representation is invalid,
trace the producer first. A guessed lookup table or consumer converter changes the contract
and can mask the source defect.

## 11. A service returns an amount in the wrong format

Capture the value at the producer boundary and compare it with the agreed representation.
If the producer violates it, correct the producer in the approved scope and verify the affected
consumer path. Check current consumers and any code that already compensates for the value.
If the correction has broad downstream impact or callers may rely on the old output, give the
owner examples of affected callers and the compatibility options before editing. A converter
in the consumer leaves the producer fault in place and needs separate justification and approval.

## Size rule of thumb

Sketch the minimal solution first. Either of these triggers close scrutiny of the diff:

- a diff more than about 2x that estimate;
- more than about 50 production lines for a one-filter or one-check ticket.

The finding itself names the specific unrequired hunks, unless a category (a) requirement
explains the difference.
